faq.q: Are mesh motorcycle jackets safe enough for touring?
faq.a: Quality mesh jackets with Cordura or ballistic nylon in impact zones and CE Level 2 armour provide about 70-80% of the abrasion resistance of solid textile jackets. For road touring at sensible speeds, this is acceptable protection, but track riding or aggressive mountain passes warrant full textile or leather.

faq.q: Can you wear a mesh jacket in the rain?
faq.a: Mesh jackets handle light drizzle for 15-20 minutes but you'll get soaked in proper British rain within five minutes. Always carry a packable waterproof layer in your pannier as backup for summer tours.

faq.q: What temperature is too cold for a mesh motorcycle jacket?
faq.a: Below 15°C, even with a thermal liner, mesh jackets struggle to keep you warm. The sweet spot is 18-30°C for comfortable riding. Early morning and evening rides often require a standard textile jacket even in summer.

faq.q: How long do mesh motorcycle jackets typically last?
faq.a: Premium jackets (£300+) last 4-5 seasons with proper care, mid-range options (£180-£280) give 3-4 seasons, while budget jackets under £150 typically manage 2 seasons before mesh separation or zipper failure. Regular inspection and proper storage extend longevity.

faq.q: Do I need to size up for a mesh motorcycle jacket?
faq.a: Yes, sizing slightly up from your usual jacket size allows for layering options—thermal liner for cool mornings, just a t-shirt for hot afternoons. Use adjustment straps at waist, biceps, and forearms to eliminate flapping while maintaining flexibility for layers.

faq.q: What should I wear under a mesh motorcycle jacket?
faq.a: Never ride with mesh directly against skin—wind chill will freeze you even on warm days. Use a moisture-wicking base layer as minimum, with a thin fleece mid-layer available for temperature drops. Cotton t-shirts absorb sweat and cause chilling when you stop.

content:
Why I Swear by Mesh Jackets for British Summer Touring

I've spent the last few summers carving through the Yorkshire Dales and sweating my way along the A9 in full textile jackets, and I can tell you this: nothing beats a proper mesh motorcycle jacket when the temperature climbs above 20°C. I know what you're thinking—Britain and hot weather don't exactly go hand in hand—but those scorching July days stuck in traffic on the M25 or crawling through the Lake District villages will have you boiling in a standard jacket.

Here's the thing about mesh jackets that took me a while to properly understand: they're not just summer jackets. They're ventilation systems you wear. The airflow through a quality mesh jacket transforms those humid British summer days from an endurance test into actually enjoyable riding. I've tested half a dozen different mesh jackets over the past three years, from budget options that fell apart after one season to premium pieces that've become my go-to gear from May through September.

What Actually Makes a Mesh Jacket Worth Buying

Right, let's cut through the marketing nonsense. A mesh jacket is essentially a textile jacket where large sections of the outer shell are replaced with—you guessed it—mesh panels. These panels let air flow directly through to your body while maintaining the structural integrity needed to hold armour and provide abrasion resistance where it matters most.

The critical areas you need to focus on are the shoulders, elbows, and back. These are your high-impact zones, and this is where quality mesh jackets separate themselves from the cheap rubbish. I've seen jackets with mesh covering 70% of the surface, which sounds brilliant until you realize the mesh is placed exactly where you'd slide in a fall. Not ideal.

Construction Details That Actually Matter

When I'm examining a mesh jacket in the shop or ordering from SportsBikeShop, I look for these specific features:

  • Ballistic nylon or Cordura in impact zones: The shoulders, elbows, forearms, and back should be solid, abrasion-resistant material, not mesh
  • Double or triple stitching: Pull on the seams. If they feel flimsy, they are flimsy
  • CE Level 2 armour as standard: Don't settle for those foam inserts masquerading as protection
  • Removable thermal liner: British mornings start cold even in July, trust me on this
  • Waterproof membrane compatibility: Some jackets have pockets for rain liners; some don't. Guess which ones are more useful in Britain
  • Adjustable vents: Being able to close off some airflow makes the jacket more versatile

How Mesh Jackets Actually Perform on British Roads

I properly tested my current mesh jacket during a week-long tour from the Cotswolds up through the Peak District and across to North Wales. Temperature swings from 14°C morning starts to 28°C afternoon riding gave me the full spectrum of British summer conditions. Here's what I learned.

At motorway speeds—let's say 70mph on the M6—the airflow is frankly intense. You'll feel every bit of wind cutting through, which is exactly what you want when you're stuck in that hellish stretch past Birmingham in afternoon heat. But drop below 40mph in town centres or slow-moving tourist traffic (looking at you, Windermere), and the ventilation becomes less effective. You're relying more on passive airflow than forced ventilation.

The sweet spot for mesh jackets is steady riding between 45-70mph in temperatures above 18°C. That's your A-road touring, your NC500 complete journey in summer, your weekday blasts through the Brecon Beacons. Below 18°C, you'll want that thermal liner in place, and honestly, below 15°C, I'm reaching for my standard textile jacket instead.

The Rain Reality Check

Let's address the elephant in the room: British weather is unpredictable at best, absolutely mental at worst. I've been caught in torrential downpours in mesh jackets more times than I can count, and here's the brutal truth—you will get wet. Very wet.

Most mesh jackets claim to have water-resistant properties. What this actually means is they'll handle light drizzle for about 20 minutes before you start feeling damp. A proper summer thunderstorm? You're soaked within five minutes. This is why I never tour without a packable rain layer in my pannier. Some riders carry a waterproof oversuit; I prefer a lightweight rain jacket that fits over my mesh jacket. It's not elegant, but neither is arriving at your destination looking like you've jumped in a lake.

A mesh jacket excels in one specific job: keeping you cool in warm weather. Ask it to do anything else, and you'll need backup solutions. Plan accordingly.

My Current Top Picks for 2026

I'm not going to pretend I've tested every single mesh jacket on the market—I'm one bloke with a bike and a limited budget—but I've ridden extensively in several models that represent different price points and approaches to mesh jacket design.

Premium Option: The Investment Piece

The high-end mesh jackets I've tested—we're talking £300-£450 range—offer features you genuinely notice. Better armour that doesn't shift around, superior fit that doesn't flap at speed, and construction quality that survives multiple seasons of hard use. The zippers work smoothly, the closures don't fail, and the materials don't degrade after a summer in the sun.

What you're paying for is longevity and refinement. My premium mesh jacket is on its fourth season and still performs like new. The cheaper jacket I tried first? Mesh started separating from the shell panels after 18 months. Do the maths on cost-per-wear, and the expensive jacket actually worked out cheaper.

Mid-Range Sweet Spot

The £180-£280 bracket is where I think most riders should focus their attention. You're getting proper CE Level 2 armour, solid construction, and enough features to handle varied conditions. The materials might not be quite as refined as the premium options, but they'll still last you several seasons of regular use.

I've found jackets in this range work brilliantly for weekend touring and summer commuting. They're good enough that you don't feel compromised on safety, but not so expensive that you're paranoid about leaving the bike in a pub car park while you grab lunch.

Budget Conscious: What You Can Get Away With

Below £150, you're making compromises. That's not necessarily a deal-breaker if you understand what you're sacrificing. Budget mesh jackets typically use lighter materials, cheaper zippers, and Level 1 armour. The fit is usually more generic, which means more flapping at speed and less comfort over long distances.

That said, I've seen budget jackets perform admirably for occasional summer use. If you're only planning a couple of week-long tours per year and primarily ride in cooler conditions, a budget mesh jacket as a supplementary piece makes sense. Just don't expect it to last beyond two seasons of regular use.

Fit, Sizing, and the Layering Challenge

Here's where loads of riders get it wrong: they size a mesh jacket like they'd size a leather jacket. Bad idea. Mesh jackets need to accommodate multiple layers—thermal liner for cool mornings, just a t-shirt for hot afternoons—while still fitting properly when you're tucked in on the bike.

I typically size up slightly from my usual jacket size, then use the adjustment straps to dial in the fit. Most quality mesh jackets have adjustment points at the waist, biceps, and forearms. Use them. A properly adjusted mesh jacket shouldn't flap like a sail at motorway speeds, but you should still be able to fit a thin fleece underneath for those cold morning starts.

When you're trying on a mesh jacket, actually get in a riding position. Reach for the bars. Check that the armour stays in place over your shoulders and elbows. Too many riders stand upright in front of a mirror, decide it looks alright, and then discover the shoulder armour migrates halfway down their biceps when they're actually riding.

Practical Tips from Years of Mesh Jacket Use

Some lessons I've learned the hard way so you don't have to:

  • Always wear something underneath: Mesh against bare skin at 60mph creates a wind chill that'll have you freezing even on warm days. A moisture-wicking base layer is your friend
  • Clean the mesh panels regularly: They accumulate road grime and dead insects like you wouldn't believe. A soft brush and mild soap solution works wonders
  • Check the armour positioning before every long ride: Armour shifts during washing and storage. Two minutes adjusting it properly could save your shoulders
  • Pack that rain layer: Seriously. British weather will betray you. I carry a packable rain jacket on every summer ride
  • Store it properly in winter: Hang it up; don't compress it in a bag. The mesh panels can deform if stored badly
  • Upgrade the back protector: Most jackets come with basic back protection. Spending £40-£60 on a proper CE Level 2 back protector is money well spent

When Mesh Jackets Aren't the Answer

I love my mesh jacket, but it's not appropriate for every situation. Early morning rides before 9am, even in summer, often start too cold for mesh. Late evening rides after 8pm? Same issue. Anything involving motorway services stops where you'll be off the bike for 20 minutes—you'll freeze without a top layer to throw on.

Long-distance touring like the Island to Highlands route requires more versatility than a mesh jacket alone provides. I typically pack both my mesh jacket and a standard textile jacket for trips longer than three days, choosing each morning based on the forecast. Yes, it takes up pannier space, but being comfortable makes every ride better.

The Ventilation vs Protection Balance

Here's the uncomfortable truth about mesh jackets: maximum ventilation and maximum protection are opposing goals. Physics doesn't care about your comfort preferences. Air flowing through the jacket means less material between you and the tarmac.

Quality manufacturers handle this by strategically placing mesh panels on areas less likely to contact the road in a slide—inner arms, sides of the torso, upper back away from the spine. The impact zones—outer shoulders, outer elbows, lower back—remain solid textile with proper abrasion resistance.

I've seen test data showing good mesh jackets provide about 70-80% of the abrasion resistance of equivalent solid textile jackets. That's the trade-off you're making for staying cool. For me, on British summer roads where I'm riding at sane speeds on familiar routes, that's acceptable. For track days or aggressive mountain pass riding? I want the full protection of solid textile or leather.

Accessorizing Your Mesh Jacket Setup

A mesh jacket is part of a system, not a complete solution. Here's what I run with mine:

  • Moisture-wicking base layer: Makes a massive difference in comfort. Cotton t-shirts get soaked with sweat and then chill you when you stop
  • Thin mid-layer fleece: Lives in my pannier for cool mornings and evenings
  • Packable rain jacket: Lightweight, stuffs into a bag the size of a grapefruit, saves the day when weather turns
  • Neck tube or summer balaclava: Stops that annoying gap between helmet and collar that creates a wind tunnel
  • Upgraded back protector: The standard foam inserts most jackets come with are frankly inadequate

Maintenance and Longevity

Mesh jackets require a bit more attention than standard textiles. The mesh panels can snag on Velcro, zippers, and rough surfaces. I've learned to turn mine inside out before washing, use a delicate cycle, and never tumble dry it. Air drying is essential—heat can damage the mesh structure and any waterproofing treatments on the solid panels.

Every few months, I inspect the stitching where mesh panels join solid panels. This is the stress point where failures typically begin. If you spot loose threads, get them repaired immediately. A small separation becomes a large hole very quickly once it starts.

The armour also needs regular inspection. Check that the foam or hard shell inserts haven't degraded, that they still fit properly in their pockets, and that the pockets haven't developed tears. I replace armour every three years as a matter of course, regardless of visible wear.

Making Your Decision

So should you buy a mesh jacket? If you regularly ride in temperatures above 20°C, absolutely. If your riding is mainly spring, autumn, and winter, probably not. If you're planning summer tours and long-distance riding when the weather's warm, it's one of the best investments you can make in riding comfort.

Start by honestly assessing how much warm-weather riding you actually do. Check your ride logs from last year. If you're doing more than 1,000 miles between May and September, a mesh jacket will transform those rides. Less than that, and you might be better served by a good textile jacket with large vents.

When you're ready to buy, visit a shop if possible and try on multiple brands. Fit varies enormously between manufacturers. What works perfectly for your mate might be completely wrong for your body shape. If you're ordering online from retailers like SportsBikeShop, check their return policy carefully and order two sizes if you're between measurements.

Your Action Plan

Right, enough theory. Here's what you actually need to do:

First, check last year's riding patterns. Look at when you rode, what temperatures you encountered, and whether you remember being uncomfortably hot. That'll tell you whether a mesh jacket solves a real problem for you or whether you're buying gear you don't actually need.

Second, set a realistic budget. Factor in the cost of upgraded armour, a proper base layer, and a rain solution. A £200 jacket might actually cost £280 once you've got it properly sorted.

Third, before using our packing checklist for your next tour, consider how a mesh jacket changes your luggage requirements. You'll need fewer cooling solutions but more layering options.

Finally, remember that gear is only valuable if you actually use it. A mesh jacket sitting in your wardrobe because it's "too nice" to risk is money wasted. Buy something you'll actually wear, maintain it properly, and it'll serve you brilliantly for years of summer touring across Britain's best roads.

Now get out there and enjoy those warm days we get about three weeks per year. Make them count.
